LanguageData.HypovolemicShock.label: hypovolemic shock
LanguageData.HypovolemicShock.description:
A life-threatening state caused by insufficient blood flow to the body. Hypovolemic shock is a medical emergency; if left untreated, the insufficient blood flow can cause damage to organs, leading to hypoxia and multiple organ failure.

Shock develops when blood loss exceeds 45%. Severity changes gradually with the remaining blood-volume deficit. Stopping the bleeding prevents further loss; restoring blood volume with transfusions or IV fluids allows recovery. The quality of shock tending determines how much it slows worsening, assists recovery, and reduces hypoxia risk. Sustained severe shock can also build acidosis before new organ injuries appear. Adrenaline buys time without lowering the underlying shock target. Existing injuries and complications still require treatment.

With delayed vital failure enabled, sustained severe shock also steadily increases cerebral hypoxia. Good shock tending and adrenaline can slow this perfusion-related damage, but do not replace missing blood.
